passage:
Ritu,
At the reunion you asked, "So what are you building these days?" and I laughed and said, "My loan repayment history." Everyone laughed. I've been thinking about it for a week.
Honest answer: nothing. I get to the office at 9:40, do the same reconciliations, eat the same paneer roll, watch two episodes and sleep. The salary is good. The flat is comfortable. Ma thinks her daughter has it all sorted. I'm not unhappy, exactly. I'm just flat. When you talked about your library project in the village, I felt something close to jealousy, and then nothing, which was worse.
I don't think I'm lazy. I work hard. It's just that everything I do comes back to me: my money, my comfort, my weekend. There's nobody else in it.
Can we talk on Saturday?
Kalyani

qa.a: "My loan repayment history."

qa.q: What did Kalyani feel when Ritu talked about the library project?
qa.a: She felt something close to jealousy and then nothing, which worried her more because it showed how flat she had become.

qa.q: What first step does asking Ritu to talk on Saturday suggest?
qa.a: Naming the flatness to a friend is a first move outward; talking could help Kalyani find one thing to care about beyond her own comfort.

qa.q: How might Ritu feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Ritu may feel trusted and a little concerned, and glad Kalyani answered honestly instead of joking again.

passage: Kishore, you'll laugh, but your question at Diwali is still stuck in my head. "What are you building, Ujjwal?" I said, "A fixed deposit." Funny, right? But here's my week. Office at ten, the same three dashboards, lunch at my desk, gym at seven, food delivery, a series, sleep. Weekend: sleep more, the mall with my flatmates. My salary goes up every year. Ma calls me her comfortable son. And I am comfortable. I'm not lazy either; I clear every target. It's just that when you asked, I saw that every single thing on that list is about me. My body, my money, my screen. Nobody's life is different because I'm in it. The feeling isn't sad, exactly. It's more like a room with no windows. Anyway. Pass the biscuits.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal answer when Kishore asked what he was building?
qa.a: "A fixed deposit."

qa.q: What feeling is Ujjwal describing with "a room with no windows"?
qa.a: A closed-in flatness: comfortable but cut off, because everything in his life points back at himself.

qa.q: What could Ujjwal try as one small change?

qa.q: How might Kishore feel hearing this answer to a Diwali question?

passage: I'm Jahnavi, Akash's older sister, and I've shared this flat with him for two years. From outside, his life looks fine. He leaves at 9:15, comes back at seven, orders the same biryani every Friday, and the salary slip he leaves on the table gets bigger each April. He isn't lazy; he has never missed a day. Last Sunday our cousin's six-year-old asked him, "What do you make at your job?" Akash opened his mouth, closed it and said, "Money." The kid lost interest. Akash didn't. He sat on the balcony for a long time without his phone, which he never does. I don't know what he was thinking. But on Monday he asked me, quite casually, what my weekend teaching class was like.

qa.a: "Money."

qa.a: The question seems to have unsettled him, maybe leaving him feeling flat or wondering what he is really building, though Jahnavi can't be sure.

qa.q: What turning point does Akash's Monday question suggest, and how could Jahnavi help?
qa.a: It hints he is looking beyond his routine; Jahnavi could invite him to her teaching class once, with no pressure.

qa.q: How does Jahnavi see her brother's life?

passage:
Monday. Anjali, twenty-five, reached the insurance office at 9:40, processed the same claim forms as always, ate lunch at her desk, and was home by half past six for an episode of her series and dal from the corner shop. It was comfortable. Her salary had gone up in April. She told herself that was enough.
Thursday. At a friend's housewarming, Joseph, from her college batch, talked about the evening literacy class he had started. Then he asked, "What are you building these days, Anjali?" She laughed. "My savings." On the way home it didn't feel funny. She felt flat, like a room with the windows shut.
Sunday. She tried to list things she had done last month that weren't for herself, and stopped at the empty page. She wasn't lazy; she worked hard. Everything just pointed inward. She left the notebook open on the table.

qa.q: What did Anjali answer when Joseph asked what she was building?
qa.a: She laughed and said, 'My savings.'

qa.q: Why did Anjali's joke stop feeling funny on the way home?
qa.a: She realised her life was comfortable but pointed only at herself, which left her feeling flat, like a room with the windows shut.

qa.q: What small step might Anjali take after staring at the empty page?
qa.a: She could ask Joseph about his literacy class, or choose one thing each week to do for someone else, opening a window outward.

qa.q: How might Joseph see Anjali's 'My savings' answer?
qa.a: He may take it as a joke without guessing how flat it left her, or he may sense something unsaid behind the laugh.

grounding: Over a week a hardworking young woman settled in comfort realises her life points only inward and feels flat when asked what she is building.

passage:
"Wasim, young man, you told me work is 'fine, just boring' and you only look forward to payday. Let your Devika Aunty from next door tell you about herself at twenty-five.
I was a clerk at the electricity office. Good salary, fixed hours, a new pressure cooker every Diwali, and every evening the radio and bed. I wasn't lazy. I was punctual; I never took a day off. But one evening my father asked, 'What are you building, Devika?' and I had nothing to say. I felt as flat as the ledger on my desk.
It took me two more years to notice that everything I did was for me: my comfort, my salary, my Sundays. A life folded in on itself.
I'm not telling you what to do. I'm only saying that if the question makes you feel flat too, it's worth listening to."

qa.q: Where did Devika Aunty work at twenty-five?
qa.a: She was a clerk at the electricity office.

qa.q: How did Devika feel when her father asked what she was building?
qa.a: She felt empty and flat, as flat as the ledger on her desk, because she had nothing to say.

qa.q: What does Devika suggest Wasim do with his own flat feeling?
qa.a: To listen to it as a sign rather than ignore it, since it took her two years to notice her life had folded inward.

qa.q: What might Devika's father have hoped she would see when he asked, 'What are you building, Devika?'
qa.a: He may have wanted her to look past the good salary and comfort and ask whether her days were adding up to anything.

grounding: An elder recalls being a punctual, comfortable young clerk whose life had turned entirely inward, and feeling flat when asked what she was building.

passage: At the Kartik mela in their small town, Indu bought jalebis for her cousin Nikita and watched the giant wheel go round. Indu, twenty-five, had been a clerk at the cooperative bank for three years. Same desk, same passbooks, same bus home by five-thirty, TV serials by eight. She liked it. It was safe. Nikita, seventeen, was full of plans: a nursing course, a stall selling her aunt's pickles, maybe a blog. "What about you, Didi? What are you building?" Indu opened her mouth and nothing came out. She thought of her salary, her new fridge, the sofa set she was saving for. None of it felt like an answer. A strange flatness settled over her, even with the lights and the loudspeaker music all around. "I don't know," she finally said, and bit into a jalebi that suddenly tasted too sweet.

qa.q: How long has Indu been a clerk at the cooperative bank?
qa.a: Indu has been a clerk there for three years.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling when Nikita asked what she was building?
qa.a: Indu felt flat and unsettled, realising she had no answer beyond her salary and comforts.

qa.q: What could Indu try after this evening?
qa.a: Indu could think about one small thing beyond her own comfort she might grow or help with, perhaps even helping Nikita with the pickle stall.

qa.q: How might Nikita see Indu's answer?
qa.a: Nikita, full of plans herself, might be puzzled or a little worried by Indu's silence, not seeing it as laziness but as something missing.

passage: Zanele had been in Addis Ababa for two days and already had a list: coffee ceremony, the museum, a jazz bar. Abebe showed her his flat: new television, nice sofa, a fridge full of ready meals. He worked at an insurance office, nine to five, and was proud of never taking work home. Over coffee Zanele asked, "So what are you building, Abebe? Remember the youth football league you wanted to start?" He laughed, then didn't. He tried to answer. His days were fine: office, gym, a series, sleep. Nothing was wrong. But hearing himself describe it, he felt oddly empty, like a room with nothing on the walls. "I don't know," he admitted. "I think I just stopped looking up." Zanele didn't lecture. She just asked if the old field near his school still existed.

passage:
At the insurance office in Pune, Tejas had been in the same job for three years. He arrived at nine, left at six, watched videos until midnight, and repeated.
At the Friday team lunch, his colleague Zeenat asked, "What are you working towards, Tejas? Any big plans?"
Tejas shrugged. "Salary hike in April. A bigger TV maybe."
"And beyond that?"
He opened his mouth and nothing came. He felt oddly flat, like a balloon a week after the party.
Zeenat talked about teaching kids on weekends, and her plan to start a small design studio.
Tejas nodded politely. Walking back to his desk, he couldn't remember the last time he'd made something, or helped anyone, or wanted anything beyond comfort.

qa.a: A salary hike.

qa.a: He felt oddly flat and empty, like a balloon a week after the party.

qa.a: Try something that builds or helps, like joining Zeenat's weekend teaching or starting a small project he cares about.

qa.a: Zeenat might be surprised or a little concerned that he has nothing beyond a salary hike and a TV.

passage:
Dear Trisha,
You asked how I am. Honestly? Fine, on paper.
The job at the bank is stable. The salary is good. I've bought a new sofa and I watch series every night. I'm not unhappy.
But at my cousin's wedding, an old teacher asked, "Arohi, what are you building now?" I didn't have an answer. I said, "My savings?" and laughed. She didn't.
It's been bothering me. Every day is the same. I don't create anything. I don't help anyone. I just want the weekend to come.
I'm not lazy. I work hard. But it's all for me.
Do you ever feel like that? What did you do?
Arohi

qa.a: Arohi has felt bothered and flat, realising there's nothing being built beyond personal comfort.

passage: Thomas, you say you're bored of your job and everything is fine. Let me tell you about me at twenty-five, in the railway accounts office in Madras. I had a permanent post, a scooter and a routine you could set a clock by. Tea at eleven, lunch at one, cinema on Saturday. I thought life was sorted. Then at my cousin's wedding, my old headmaster asked, 'Ramesh, what are you making with all this time?' I made a joke. But I lay awake. I wasn't lazy; I was just pointed entirely at myself. The next month I started teaching accounts free on Sunday mornings to boys from the railway colony who couldn't afford tuition. Forty years later, three of those boys are chartered accountants. One named his son after me. That's the only part of my twenties I talk about.

qa.q: What did the old headmaster ask Ramesh?
qa.a: 'Ramesh, what are you making with all this time?'

qa.q: How did Ramesh feel lying awake after the headmaster's question?
qa.a: Ramesh felt unsettled and a little empty, realising the comfortable life pointed only inward.

qa.q: Ramesh started teaching accounts free on Sunday mornings. Why was that a turning point?
qa.a: It turned Ramesh's life outward, using a skill for boys who couldn't afford tuition, and grew something beyond the self.

qa.q: How might the boys from the railway colony have seen those Sunday classes?
qa.a: They probably felt grateful and hopeful, finally getting help they couldn't pay for, which shaped their careers.

grounding: An elder recalls a comfortable, inward routine at twenty-five, the flatness a question exposed, and turning outward.

passage: The power cut hit the Pune flat at 7 pm and showed no sign of ending. Tejas's phone died at 7:40. Without a screen, the evening stretched ahead of him like an empty road. His life had been smooth for two years: a good salary at the software firm, the gym, weekend brunches, a new bike on instalments. He had been proud of how comfortable it was. Now, sitting in the dark, he tried to think of one thing he was building that wasn't for himself. Nothing came. At ten his flatmate Mridul came in with a torch, sweaty and grinning, back from the blood bank where he volunteered on Thursdays. 'Fourteen donors tonight,' Mridul said. Tejas said, 'Nice,' and felt something sink. He wasn't a bad person. He had just stopped looking outward. 'Can I come next Thursday?' he asked.

qa.q: Where does Mridul volunteer on Thursdays?
qa.a: At the blood bank.

qa.q: What did Tejas feel when Mridul said 'Fourteen donors tonight'?
qa.a: Tejas felt something sink, a flat, empty feeling at realising he was building nothing beyond himself.

qa.q: What did Tejas do right at the end of the evening?
qa.a: He asked to join Mridul next Thursday, taking a first small step outward instead of just feeling bad.

qa.q: How might Mridul react to Tejas asking to come?
qa.a: Mridul would probably be pleased and welcoming, glad to share something that clearly lifts his own evenings.

passage: Navratri nights in Ahmedabad used to mean garba till two for Anjali. This year she came home from the office at six, ordered paneer rolls and watched three episodes of a baking show. Her salary had gone up again in April. The flat was comfortable. On Dussehra, at the society dinner, her old classmate Chetan was glowing about the school library he and some friends were setting up in his village. "And you? What are you building these days?" Anjali opened her mouth. Her mind went to the new sofa. "Oh, the usual, work's good," she said, and it came out thin. Walking home past the empty garba ground, she felt oddly flat, not tired exactly. She did not know what she wanted to build. She hadn't asked herself in two years.
